~~~
  function change_stream_privacy(e, url, success_message, error_message, invite_only, is_private) {
        e.preventDefault();

        var stream_id = $(e.target).closest(".subscription_settings").attr("data-stream-id");
        var sub = stream_data.get_sub_by_id(stream_id);

        $("#subscriptions-status").hide();
        var data = {stream_name: sub.name, privacy: is_private};

        channel.patch({
            url: url,
            data: data,
            success: function () {
                sub = stream_data.get_sub_by_id(stream_id);
                var stream_settings = settings_for_sub(sub);
                var sub_row = $(".stream-row[data-stream-id='" + stream_id + "']");
                sub.invite_only = invite_only;
                redraw_privacy_related_stuff(sub_row, sub);
                var feedback_div = stream_settings.find(".change-stream-privacy-feedback").expectOne();
                ui.report_success(success_message, feedback_div);
            },
            error: function (xhr) {
                var stream_settings = settings_for_sub(sub);
                var feedback_div = stream_settings.find(".change-stream-privacy-feedback").expectOne();
                ui.report_error(error_message, xhr, feedback_div);
            }
        });
    }

    $("#subscriptions_table").on("click", ".make-stream-public-button", function (e) {
        change_stream_privacy(
            e,
            "/json/streams/" + sub.name,
            "The stream has been made public!",
            "Error making stream public",
            false,
            false
        );
    });

    $("#subscriptions_table").on("click", ".make-stream-private-button", function (e) {
        change_stream_privacy(
            e,
            "/json/streams/" + sub.name,
            "The stream has been made private!",
            "Error making stream private",
            true,
            true
        );
    });
~~~

function change_stream_privacy(e, is_private, success_message, error_message, invite_only) {
        e.preventDefault();

        var stream_id = $(e.target).closest(".subscription_settings").attr("data-stream-id");
        var sub = stream_data.get_sub_by_id(stream_id);

        $("#subscriptions-status").hide();
        var data = {stream_name: sub.name, privacy: is_private};

        if is_private:
            mode = '/public'
        else:
            mode = '/private'

        channel.patch({
            url: "/json/streams/" + sub.name + mode,
            data: data,
            success: function () {
                sub = stream_data.get_sub_by_id(stream_id);
                var stream_settings = settings_for_sub(sub);
                var sub_row = $(".stream-row[data-stream-id='" + stream_id + "']");
                sub.invite_only = invite_only;
                redraw_privacy_related_stuff(sub_row, sub);
                var feedback_div = stream_settings.find(".change-stream-privacy-feedback").expectOne();
                ui.report_success(success_message, feedback_div);
            },
            error: function (xhr) {
                var stream_settings = settings_for_sub(sub);
                var feedback_div = stream_settings.find(".change-stream-privacy-feedback").expectOne();
                ui.report_error(error_message, xhr, feedback_div);
            }
        });
~~~

well has_request_variables is the decorator, and the @ syntax calls it

**Sampriti Panda** · 2016-12-23 13:47 UTC

what that does is, it takes all the arguments of the view function which are assigned objects of class REQ as a default argument and assigns them with their value from the the request data.

**Sampriti Panda** · 2016-12-23 13:47 UTC

so for example you have `is_private=REQ()`

**Sampriti Panda** · 2016-12-23 13:47 UTC

now has_request_variables will takes the value of is_private from whatever you passed in the request (in the JS code) and calls the function with that value.

## translate bot

*2017-01-14 to 2017-01-14 · 20 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/91-code-review/topic/translate.20bot/with/127940)*

**Roy Abouhamad** · 2017-01-14 14:38 UTC

Hi can someone please have a look at my translate bot.

**Roy Abouhamad** · 2017-01-14 14:38 UTC

https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/3314

**Abhay Kashyap** · 2017-01-14 14:44 UTC

How do you run the bot?

**Abhay Kashyap** · 2017-01-14 14:44 UTC

What should I send the message as to activate the bot?

**Abhay Kashyap** · 2017-01-14 14:44 UTC

And also, which stream should I send the message in?

**Abhay Kashyap** · 2017-01-14 14:44 UTC

Private or the other streams?

**Roy Abouhamad** · 2017-01-14 14:45 UTC

You can send the message to any stream in the dev environment as long as the bot is subscribed to that stream

**Roy Abouhamad** · 2017-01-14 14:46 UTC

It also works if you send the message to the bot as a private message

**Roy Abouhamad** · 2017-01-14 14:47 UTC

However you must first create a bot in the settings of the dev environment and download the .zuliprc-local file rename it to '.zuliprc-local' as it is originally called unknown and place it in your base folder

**Roy Abouhamad** · 2017-01-14 14:48 UTC

Then run ```python run.py lib/translate.py --config-file ~/.zuliprc-local```

**Roy Abouhamad** · 2017-01-14 14:48 UTC

messages follow the format ```@translate <word> <translate_code>```

OK thanks!

**Summary of the fix:**
* Prevents the “phantom notification dot” caused by browser favicon caching (especially in Chromium-based browsers).
* Resets the favicon on `pagehide` to avoid caching the dotted state.
* Handles bfcache restores via `pageshow` to correctly reapply the unread state if needed.

## upgrade hashing algorithm

*2017-02-02 to 2017-02-02 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/91-code-review/topic/upgrade.20hashing.20algorithm/with/143859)*

**sinwar** · 2017-02-02 21:58 UTC

I made this PR #3410
Please check it out @Steve Howell @Tim Abbott

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-02 22:02 UTC

Is there some Django thing that I don't know about that requires us to have four fallback hashers even if we install argon?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-02 22:02 UTC

(This is not a rhetorical question. ^^^^ I am asking out of ignorance on my part.)

**sinwar** · 2017-02-02 22:20 UTC

In django default password hasher is
```
PASSWORD_HASHERS = [
    'django.contrib.auth.hashers.PBKDF2PasswordHasher',
    'django.contrib.auth.hashers.PBKDF2SHA1PasswordHasher',
    'django.contrib.auth.hashers.Argon2PasswordHasher',
    'django.contrib.auth.hashers.BCryptSHA256PasswordHasher',
    'django.contrib.auth.hashers.BCryptPasswordHasher',
]
```
now we are upgrading to argon 
```
PASSWORD_HASHERS = [
    'django.contrib.auth.hashers.Argon2PasswordHasher',
    'django.contrib.auth.hashers.PBKDF2PasswordHasher',
    'django.contrib.auth.hashers.PBKDF2SHA1PasswordHasher',
    'django.contrib.auth.hashers.BCryptSHA256PasswordHasher',
    'django.contrib.auth.hashers.BCryptPasswordHasher',
]
```
as per https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/1.10/topics/auth/passwords/

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-02 22:21 UTC

I think we only need as fallbacks ones that we've used in the past

**sinwar** · 2017-02-02 22:23 UTC

by default we've used ```PBKDF2```

**sinwar** · 2017-02-02 22:23 UTC

in past

**sinwar** · 2017-02-02 22:24 UTC

yes you are right because fallback ones are for checking purpose and there is no meaning to check against except past algorithm

**sinwar** · 2017-02-02 22:26 UTC

updated

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-02 22:32 UTC

Oh, I think I get it now--we would have to re-hash all of our old passwords to move to just using one new hasher, and of course that's impossible, since we only stored the hashed password.

**sinwar** · 2017-02-02 22:34 UTC

Nope djanago will restore password with new hash when users log in and another hasher is for check password when new hasher doesn't recognize user password.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-02 22:35 UTC

So Django basically upgrades your hash to a new algorithm every time you human-enter a correct password?

**sinwar** · 2017-02-02 22:36 UTC

yup

**sinwar** · 2017-02-02 22:37 UTC

https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/1.10/topics/auth/passwords/#password-upgrading

## muting perf #3605

*2017-02-08 to 2017-02-11 · 16 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/91-code-review/topic/muting.20perf.20.233605/with/146806)*

**Elliott Jin** · 2017-02-08 10:01 UTC

Hello, I submitted a PR for issue #3605 here: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/3614 but I just wanted to double check: am I correct in assuming that unread.update_unread_counts() only needs to be called once (instead of once per topic)?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-08 17:00 UTC

yeah, it should only need to be called once

**Elliott Jin** · 2017-02-08 19:25 UTC

@Steve Howell Thanks for reviewing this!  Sure, I'd be interested in looking at follow-up cleanup--what did you have in mind?  (I won't be able to respond immediately but I'll be on chat again later this evening.)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-08 19:26 UTC

Hi, @Elliott Jin!  Basically, what I have in mind is moving some code (and callers, of course) to unread_ui.js and muting_ui.js.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-08 19:28 UTC

Basically, we want a UI layer that does real side-effect-y things like update DOM and then a data layer that just keeps track of data stuff.  This will eventually make it a little easier to manage circular dependencies.  All the data stuff will be easy to make be "leaves" on the dependency tree (more or less).  The UI stuff will still be prone to circular dependencies, but if we keep the UI layer fairly slim, we can manage that with callbacks or other tricks to make the dependency graph acyclical.

**Elliott Jin** · 2017-02-09 07:23 UTC

OK, my current understanding of the goals are:
(1) This "side effect" code should be in a "UI layer" file, instead of in unread.js: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/static/js/unread.js#L275
(2) muting.js shouldn't have to call unread.update_unread_counts() after updating its internal data structures

Does this sound about right (e.g. am I missing any important goals)?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-09 16:42 UTC

#2 is debatable.  I think it's still ok to have interactions between the UI layers, where, for example, our muting UI code orchestrates the call to update the unread counts.  The code would ideally look something like this:

~~~
server_events.handle_muting_event:
    muting_ui.set_topics


muting_ui.set_topics:
    muting.set_topics # set data
    unread_ui.update_unread_counts

unread_ui.update_unread_counts:
    activity.update_dom_with_unread_counts
    stream_list.update_dom_with_unread_counts
    # etc.

**Elliott Jin** · 2017-02-10 07:14 UTC

here's an initial draft; is this something along the lines of what you had in mind?
https://github.com/robot-dreams/zulip/commit/7eb18b1f199ed68153ecfbafa95e518609e6d8f4

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-10 15:22 UTC

Yep, that looks basically exactly like what I was looking for!  It would be nice to break this into relatively small commits, although that can be challenging for these types of refactoring, since when you move one method, it often requires bringing a few methods along for the ride.   But we can probably break it up a little bit.

**Elliott Jin** · 2017-02-10 19:31 UTC

Sounds good--I can split it up later this evening.  Just double checking, what's the preferred way to submit these types of refactoring pull request(s)?  One pull request per commit, or one pull request containing every commit (but each commit has a reasonable commit message)?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-10 19:43 UTC

the latter -- one pull request with a series of commits.  We merge via rebase, and thus the individual, readable commits will end up in the permanent history.  Pull request descriptions are discarded

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-10 19:49 UTC

Another thing to note, which maybe goes without saying, is that each of the commits should be atomic and pass all tests, etc.

**Elliott Jin** · 2017-02-11 09:17 UTC

I've opened a pull request https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/3645 that splits the refactor into 4 commits, but please feel free to let me know if you prefer another way of splitting or different commit messages

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-11 16:37 UTC

Merged!  Thanks, @Elliott Jin!

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-11 16:41 UTC

If you find these types of cleanups rewarding/interesting, the holy grail is to tame `subs.js`.  I would start by reading it and getting a feel for the several types of responsibilities it has and see if there are some clean breaks and low hanging fruit.   Plenty of other stuff to do as well, if you want a break from refactoring.

**Elliott Jin** · 2017-02-11 17:46 UTC

Great, thanks for the help with this!  I'll be away from Zulip for the next week or so but I'm interested in continuing this discussion when I get back.

Ok, good to know.  One of the commit that @Harshit Bansal has in the PR is to make it so that we flip restricted_to_domain to False if there are no RealmAliases.  I understand the logic here--it's almost always correct in the "Do What I Mean, not what I say" sense--but it might have some edge case implications we haven't considered.  For example, I might be moving to a new domain but still want a restricted domain, and then I arbitrarily decide to delete the old domain and then re-create the new domain (rather than vice versa).

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-08 19:14 UTC

(and then the delete would turn off restricted domains, but the add would not turn on restricted domains)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-08 19:14 UTC

Hrm, yeah, I see what you mean; if you have no domains and `restricted_to_domain` on, then nobody can join.

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-02-08 19:16 UTC

@Tim Abbott That's why in that I am setting `restricted_to_domains` to false automatically.

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-02-08 19:18 UTC

@Steve Howell The delete would disable the restricted_to_domains so that we don't have a situation where we don't have any domains and restricted_to_domains to true.

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-02-08 19:19 UTC

As soon as we add some domains the restricted_to_domains checkbox will be enabled and the admin will be able to set as per his needs.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-08 19:19 UTC

Yeah I guess I'm not sure what the best strategy is here.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-08 19:23 UTC

My compromise would be to not make it too magical.  I think admins tend to like explicit control over things, even if they occasionally shoot themselves in the foot.  So I'd be more inclined to have warnings--"Hey! Do you realize nobody can join now?" (but worded more nicely)--rather than have the system try to read their mind.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-08 19:25 UTC

But I also think there's an argument that until we actually make our restriction model more complex (by adding guest users, etc.) that we should just go with what @Harshit Bansal has done on the PR.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-08 19:25 UTC

And if we go with the latter approach, we should just comment the code accordingly.

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-02-08 19:28 UTC

I think the latter approach is a bit more robust. I will add comments wherever necessary.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-08 19:30 UTC

I'm good with that.  @Tim Abbott can you give a quick sign-off on that approach before @Harshit Bansal invests too much time in commenting?

## this stream

*2017-02-27 to 2017-02-28 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/91-code-review/topic/this.20stream/with/158435)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-27 23:11 UTC

So, just a quick comment on some of the review requests on this stream.  In general, I do code review based on the GitHub notifications, not this stream, to make sure I see everything; this stream if for getting quick comments on changes you've made from another developer.  I'd really like to see more folks checking things out and posting even quick comments of the form "Seems to work!" or "this thing looks funny; can you investigate?" in addition to comments on the code.

There are sorta 2 things that can help make this a successful process:
* Folks who are asking for review should provide clarity about what they did, to make it enticing for potential reviewers.  E.g. "I added LaTeX support, it's really cool, check it out!" or "I made our alert words UI look nice again!" are great brief advertisements that are a lot better than just posting a PR ID.
* Developers, especially those new to the project, taking the time to look at others' changes, both the code and actually trying running it on their machine.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-27 23:13 UTC

We recently updated the docs in README.md to sorta advertise this model, but the project will move a lot faster if there are more folks actively doing peer review, since it frees up the time from our most experienced developers to focus on things that already have been manually tested by someone

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-28 02:35 UTC

Just to augment Tim's point, it's really effective to post a specific question on this stream.  Example messages:

* "This is my first PR, and I need a high level review to make sure I'm on the right track."
* "I feel confident in the code change, but I'm having problems writing a good test due to jQuery interactions."
* "I'm not a native English speaker.  Can somebody review for English?"
* "Travis failed and I don't understand what this error means."
* "My changes work, but I wonder if we should refactor foo.py as part of this change."

@Tim Abbott @Kanak Garg There's been a lot of discussion about add_sub_to_table, and let me explain the scenario, which is a bit obscure, but which I think we should eventually handle.  If I'm Cordelia, and I go into Manage Streams, then Iago creates a public stream but does not subscribe me (playing the role of Cordelia), then I should get a live update in the Manage Streams UI to add the new public stream to the list of "All Streams."  Earlier in the discussion I was under the impression that we might support that feature.  Apparently we don't, and it's not the end of the world.  But when we do support that live update, we'll need to be careful about making sure the "View Stream" button works, since you're allowed to view a public stream before subscribing to it.  Either that, or we can decide to just not show the button, on the theory that there were won't be much interesting to view when the stream is initially created.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-10 17:03 UTC

There are bunch of scenarios.  Suppose you're Hamlet, and you're not doing anything yet, but you are in "Manage Streams."  Then Iago does one of the following things:
* Iago creates a private stream without you.  (This is easy--Hamlet does not get any events here.  To Hamlet it's like nothing happened.)
* Iago creates a private stream with you.  (You may get multiple events here, and you want to avoid duplicate UI updates).
* Iago creates a public stream without you.  (You're not subscribed to the stream yet, but you do get informed that the stream now exists; this is #4015, basically.)
* Iago creates a public stream with you.  (Again, you need to be careful of redundant UI updates.)
* Iago adds you to an existing private stream.
* Iago removes you from an existing private stream.
* Iago adds you to an existing public stream.
* Iago removes you from an existing public stream.

The PR is in response to the issue  https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/3212 . It manages the unsent messages to the server(i.e when server is down). After 15s of no response from the server a small message is shown below the message informing the user that the message has not been sent. I have also created the unit tests for this. It will be great if someone can review it. PR #4112

**Mahim Goyal** · 2017-03-24 21:38 UTC

PR #4112. I have made compose unit tests for the part where message has not been received by the server. There are three scenarios that we test:
* message succeeds in time, and we need to clear the timeout timer
* message fails quickly, and we need to clear the timeout timer
* message times out before response, and we need to verify the timeout logic kicks in

For the 2nd case  `echo.message_send_error` is called in unit tests which actually calls clearTimeout. In this we check whether the timeout function is cleared or not by `echo.message_send_error`. There is some pretty interesting stuff going on here.

The commit msg linter can be maximally used if it is hooked to @zulipbot for code review. This applies to the existing code linters as well. cc: @Cynthia Lin .

**Joshua Pan** · 2017-05-13 01:20 UTC

@Rein Zustand can you elaborate?

**Joshua Pan** · 2017-05-13 01:21 UTC

It is easier to have it as a Travis test, since it'll be a Travis failure and restricts the branch from accidentally being merged.

**Rein Zustand** · 2017-05-13 01:39 UTC

I see. The Travis backend test already runs `./tools/lint --pep8`. By "maximally used", I meant being run at each commit, rather than just being run by a subset of the devs who have added the linter to the git hook.

**Joshua Pan** · 2017-05-13 01:42 UTC

How would @zulipbot play in this scenario?

**Rein Zustand** · 2017-05-13 01:55 UTC

Hmm, agreed it is easier to have it as a Travis test. Though it could be implemented in @zulipbot where it could halt the Travis test if the linter fails. I see @zulipbot as a handler to github-related (e.g. @-mentioning reviewers) tasks. The commit msg linter is a git-related task.

**Joshua Pan** · 2017-05-13 01:57 UTC

Yes, and @zulipbot really doesn't have any control over Travis (or would be harder to implement).

**Rein Zustand** · 2017-05-13 02:07 UTC

Yeah, I found that it is already in https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/cf15a7b56160663021852575fe34acb9083f9437/tools/lint#L696, but commented out. Imagine another scenario of git-related task: if the sha1 collision checker hadn't been baked into git/github yet, it would be better put into a Travis script?

**Joshua Pan** · 2017-05-13 02:08 UTC

Yea, we do have a commit msg linter, but it's still buggy and giving false positives

**Cynthia Lin** · 2017-05-13 02:42 UTC

I don't think zulipbot would have any way to cancel a Travis build or read the logs from a build, unfortunately. Like you said, zulipbot was mainly designed to integrate with the GitHub API (although we do support Travis build completion notifications with their webhooks).

**Cynthia Lin** · 2017-05-13 02:43 UTC

And yeah, I think the commit message linter we have has been commented out because of some bugs in it.

## #4323

*2017-04-04 to 2017-04-04 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/91-code-review/topic/.234323/with/184868)*

**Akyya Mayberry** · 2017-04-04 21:10 UTC

>needs help writing more concise commit message.

Can someone offer some help on this. I tried my best to follow the recommendations in the docs.

**Yago González** · 2017-04-04 21:15 UTC

Yup, here are a few tips:
* Keep the commit title (the first line in the commit's message) <= 50 characters long.
* Most of the time we use for the title the following structure: `<part>: <Brief_description>.`, where "part" is a tag that identifies which code section are you modifying (e.g. css, backend, i18n). In the case of your PR, it's probably `markdown`. Also note that the "brief description" starts with a capital letter and ends with a period.

**Yago González** · 2017-04-04 21:16 UTC

So, my advice in this case would be to use the same title you used in the PR for the commit. I think that one is concise enough, especially with the good details you've provided in the rest of the commit's message :)

**Akyya Mayberry** · 2017-04-04 21:46 UTC

Thanks. I appreciate the feedback.

## case studies

*2017-04-07 to 2017-04-07 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/91-code-review/topic/case.20studies/with/186448)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-07 14:53 UTC

@Sumana Harihareswara has asked me and Tim for a few representative PRs that she can incorporate in code review training, so when I come across them, I will post them here. Other folks may find this thread interesting as a way to learn about the process.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-07 14:56 UTC

#4449, from @Umair Khan, is an example of a solid PR where the feedback is suggestive in nature.  He made three well-worded commits that seem valid to me, and each commit has a unit test.  My suggestion is to de-duplicate the code a bit.  This is an interesting case, because there's always a little bit of tension between avoiding duplication and keeping code explicit (or another way to say it is to avoid indirection on the reader).  So it will be interesting to see how this plays out.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-07 14:57 UTC

Sumana -- you may need to capture the state of the PR before the next round of fixes (if there are any).

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-07 19:36 UTC

I think we could also grab a few examples of commits with great commit messages, and use those to improve our "commit style" documentation.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-07 20:09 UTC

There are two examples given in our current doc, with a very odd linking style.  See "these examples" in the first line here: https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/version-control.html#commit-messages

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-07 20:10 UTC

I think 4 or 5 good ones are all we really need, and they just need to be on the spectrum from "short and sweet" to "highly nuanced explanation."

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-07 22:09 UTC

gonna start a new topic for example commit messages...


## example commit messages

*2017-04-07 to 2017-04-07 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/91-code-review/topic/example.20commit.20messages/with/186602)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-07 22:11 UTC

One-liners are often sufficient:

~~~
    mypy: Fix missing documentation_crawler annotation.
    Create topic_generator.js.
    integrations doc: Move trello-plugin doc to separate file.
    hotkey: Clean up state more consistently in node tests.
    api-docs: Fix JavaScript code sample.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-07 22:12 UTC

Then the following examples will show ways to add value in follow-up paragraphs...

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-07 22:13 UTC

Explain a workaround:

~~~
    documentation_crawler: Add exclude list.

    This works around the issue that Google calendar returns errors on
    HTTP HEAD requests.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-07 22:14 UTC

Explain the decision-making that led to the patch:

~~~
    actions: Remove some unnecessary log_event calls.

    Users editing messages or updating message flags are either already
    recorded or not interesting from an audit perspective, and so there's
    no need to use log_event with them.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-07 22:15 UTC

Simply elaborate on what was hard to say in just one line:

~~~
    settings-bots: Fix bots styling to prevent content from overflowing.

    This fixes the styling of the container so that the text will not
    overflow to the next line but instead will just wrap around the
    container correctly.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-07 22:16 UTC

Pass along some useful historical knowledge (and also auto-close the issue):

~~~
    requirements: Upgrade python-twitter to latest version.

    We no longer need a forked version, since our patches were merged into
    master several months ago.

    Fixes #3407.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-07 22:17 UTC

Clarify what was actually broken (beyond just the issue number):

~~~
    settings: Fix positioning of user upload spinner.

    Previously the "Uploading" text was floating outside the upload
    widget.

    Fixes #4223.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-07 22:19 UTC

Contextualize the commit by suggesting possible follow-up actions:

~~~
    hotkeys: Handle up/down arrows in settings page.

    The up/down arrows now navigate the left pane of the settings menu.
    The code here was originally implemented as part of our settings
    redesign, but the code was added in a place that became unreachable
    after we fixed a bug with home_tab_obscured().  This commit
    resurrects the code and places the guts of it in settings.js.  It
    is possible that we want to clean this code up eventually to deal
    better with hidden blocks.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-07 22:21 UTC

Explain things about the architecture/framework:

~~~
     backends: Test authenticate() with kwargs.

     Django uses arguments to differentiate between different authenticate
     function so it is important to pass arguments in a predictable manner.
     Keyword args will test the name of the argument as well.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-07 22:22 UTC

Explain performance implications:

~~~
    Add ping_only flag for presence updates.

    The web app doesn't need any presence data for its first ping to
    the server, because it already has up-to-date presence info in
    page_params.  So now we can tell the server not to send us a big
    payload that we were already ignoring.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-04-07 22:25 UTC

Ok, that's all for now. :)  I think the moral of the story is that there are several reasons to write a follow-up paragraph, and the only common theme is that you want to "explain what's most important."

## about this stream

*2017-05-05 to 2017-05-05 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/91-code-review/topic/about.20this.20stream/with/196754)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-05 18:36 UTC

This stream (#**code review**) is intended to augment github.  If you complete a PR, it's often sufficient to just add a comment to your PR explaining your change, and it will be reviewed as part of the normal github queue.  Having said that, it can often be useful to notify people here.  If you do so, please provide some interesting context.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-05 18:38 UTC

Some example things to say about your review that can help people decide whether to engage are as follows:
* "This is an urgent bug fix!  Can I get this prioritized?"
* "Can somebody who knows a lot about the emoji system review this?"
* "This is a pretty easy PR, if a newbie wants to practice code reviews."

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-05 18:39 UTC

Another appropriate time to post here is when you've submitted a PR but have some doubts about your design.  You can post here saying you want a code review, and then get the conversation started about what you think may be flawed or tricky in your approach.

**Tejas Kasetty** · 2017-05-05 18:49 UTC

Got it. Will follow these guidelines. :thumbs_up:


## #4487

*2017-05-06 to 2017-05-06 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/91-code-review/topic/.234487/with/196961)*

**Vishnu KS** · 2017-05-06 07:41 UTC

Ready for another round of review https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/4487

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-06 13:19 UTC

I added a few comments.  For date-diff functions, it's important to think through the scenario that it's just after midnight, especially for realms like ours where people are in different time zones, so it might be interesting to me to know how many hours ago folks on the other side of the world were online.  (The concept of "yesterday" is sort of blurry for that.)

**Vishnu KS** · 2017-05-06 14:27 UTC

What if we show yesterday only if they were offline for more than 12 or 24 hours or something like so that cases like just after midnight would be handled?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-06 14:34 UTC

I feel like the cutoff should be 24 hours.  If I sometimes tell you that Alice was on 14 hours ago, then I think I should always tell you 14-hours-ago whatever the time of day is for me.

**Vishnu KS** · 2017-05-06 14:36 UTC

Okay. I will tweak the code :)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-06 14:37 UTC

one way to do this is something like this

~~~ 
minutes = time_diff(...)
if (minutes < 1) return just_now;
if (minutes < 60) { // do minutes }
hours = floor(minutes/60.0)
if (hours < 24) { // do hours }
days = floor(hours/24.0)
// do days

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-06 14:39 UTC

The approach where you keep dividing to get to bigger units simplifies things a bit, because then you don't have to worry about about rounding times down to the start of the day.

**Vishnu KS** · 2017-05-06 14:41 UTC

Yeah. This looks simpler and efficient. I will change my approach similar to this.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-06 14:44 UTC

I would also spend some extra attention on the tests.  I made some suggestions in the PR, but I think you can make the code even simpler and nicer to read.  For your tests, I think it's really helpful to have the inputs just be concrete values, rather than computing anything.  This makes things easy to read.  Examples could be something like:

~~~
var now = march_first(0, 0, 5)
var then = leap_day(11, 59, 59)
assert.same(diff(then, now), "5 minutes ago");

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-06 14:45 UTC

And then just make some nice helper functions for things like leap_day, new_years_day, and march_first.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-06 14:47 UTC

Another option for your helper functions is `fake_today` and `fake_yesterday`, where the dates are interesting dates that might reveal bugs, and where the helpers allow you to pass in hours/minutes/seconds.

What do you mean exactly with "passing a new argument to the bot's handler"? You mean to the `BotHandlerApi` object?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-11 12:21 UTC

Well, actually, only one involving `client`: The `initialize(client)` function.

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-06-11 12:24 UTC

## #5150

*2017-06-15 to 2017-06-15 · 25 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/91-code-review/topic/.235150/with/228760)*

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2017-06-15 17:00 UTC

@Tim Abbott @Steve Howell please review this once, so that I can make any needed changes.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-15 17:09 UTC

I don't know the full story behind this PR.  Personally, I think we only need a blacklist for debug mode, so that you can filter out a few of the spammier errors.  Having a whitelist just seems prone to letting bugs go through, and I think the interface is complicated to understand.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2017-06-15 17:09 UTC

Okay, so I'll simply give the option of specifying which logs to block.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-15 17:12 UTC

Do we want the decision of whether logs should be blocked to be in the blueslip library or on the line of code that does the logging?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-15 17:12 UTC

I feel like the latter is more discoverable.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2017-06-15 17:15 UTC

I was hoping that we won't ever merge any changes to the blackklist, but this would be used just while debugging.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2017-06-15 17:17 UTC

Also, IMO if you are getting logs on console you don't want to see while testing, simply adding that message type to the blacklist would be easier than refactoring the whole codebase for lines that log that message type.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-15 17:17 UTC

The convenience advantage of Rohitt's approach is that it does a string search.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-15 17:19 UTC

I'm just not completely sure we want to suppress log messages, since every developer probably has a different coping strategy for log spam.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-15 17:20 UTC

For messages that are truly spammy, we should probably just remove them or just make them a bit easier to ignore by prefacing them with some wording that makes it clear they are innocuous 99% of the time.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-18 23:03 UTC

So I've been noticing folks have fallen into bad patterns in asking for code reviews here. First, make sure you've read:
* https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contributing/reviewable-prs.html
* https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contributing/review-process.html
* https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contributing/code-reviewing.html

Also, when posting a PR for review, please make sure the message clarifies concisely what the project is, and what sort of review you need. `I opened #1234` does not make it easy for others to decide whether this is something they can help with, without first clicking and readily a bunch of context.

Whereas if you wrote a UI change, and what you need first is someone to test that it appears to match what the issue asks for because you're uncertain whether your changes work, that's something that just about anyone reading this can do.

*2017-09-06 to 2017-09-10 · 15 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/91-code-review/topic/merging.20PRs/with/277348)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-06 14:45 UTC

(cross posted from #**announce** )

Folks may have noticed that we haven't merged many PRs recently.  We have several key people on vacation this week.  Even if we were fully staffed, we would be conservative about merging changes due to the upcoming release.

I can get a few things merged this week.  If you are working on core features or large PRs, expect delays.  I am a lot more likely to merge things like **doc updates**, **small bug fixes**, **automated tests**,  and **tooling improvements**. ## #7682

*2017-12-07 to 2017-12-07 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/91-code-review/topic/.237682/with/370514)*

**Joshua Pan** · 2017-12-07 14:49 UTC

For #7682, came across the use of `stream_data.get_default_status` when you can directly test `page_params.realm_default_streams`. Which is the better idea? Pinging @Steve Howell

**Steve Howell** · 2017-12-07 14:53 UTC

Ideally we could assert both side effects there.  We want to make sure that `stream_data` works like a black box, and then we also want to make sure `page_params` gets updated.  Then, if somebody refactors later, usually only one will break, and the future person can decide if it's intentional to break it or not.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-12-07 14:55 UTC

On a related note, I generally try to avoid using `page_params` too directly.  My philosophy is that it's just a blob that comes down at page load, and then we should have our own data structures with methods to encapsulate them.  For some things, however, particularly settings, my philosophy can be overkill, so we still use page_params directly in some places and even mutate it.

**Joshua Pan** · 2017-12-07 14:56 UTC

Makes sense.

**Joshua Pan** · 2017-12-07 14:56 UTC

I do know that we usually stub `page_params` out.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-12-07 15:00 UTC

Yeah, for the node testing, it's fine to stub out `page_params` but still look at how it gets mutated in the tests.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-12-12 19:38 UTC

Get your branch to a nice clean state and then do `git branch ttt-backup`.  Then do `./tools/review 230` and then do `git rebase -i review-230`.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-12-12 19:39 UTC

That will give you a local backup and you can even push your backup branch to the cloud with `git push origin ttt-backup`, and you will also have the old HEAD commit in `git reflog`.

by "nice clean state", I just mean everything checked in, so you can do `git commit -am wip` to get clean

**Yashashvi Dave** · 2018-02-01 20:00 UTC

#8101: The concepts which is implemented in PR are,
* First one is validating private stream without stream admin on stream creation. 
On stream creation our `add_subscribers_backend` function in `streams.py` is called. As this function is not called only on creating stream, we should only add this restriction to newly created stream. which is :
```python
    for stream in created_streams:
        # You can not create private stream without stream admin.
        if stream.invite_only and len(stream_admin_ids) == 0:
                return json_error(_("Private stream must require at least one admin."))
```
* The second validation is stream admin must be subscribed to stream. So, we are again validating `add_subscribers_backend` function to check that the stream admins are subscribed to stream or not. If they are not subscribed then we should also check that whether they are in `subscribers` list(list of users to subscribe to stream). So this will enables the scenario like subscribe-user-and-make-user-stream-admin in call, by passing user in both list `subscribers` and `stream_admins`.
```python
    # Check if stream admin subscribed to stream or not.
    stream_ids = set([stream.id for stream in streams])
    for stream_admin in stream_admins:
        # If stream admin is not already subscribed to stream and not included
        # in subscribers list, raise an error.
        admin_subscribed_streams = do_get_streams(stream_admin, include_default=True)
        admin_subscribed_stream_ids = set([admin_subscribed_stream['stream_id']
                                          for admin_subscribed_stream in admin_subscribed_streams])
        if stream_admin not in subscribers and not admin_subscribed_stream_ids.issubset(stream_ids):
            return json_error(_("Stream admin '%s' must subscribe to stream.") % (stream_admin.email))

```

**Yashashvi Dave** · 2018-02-01 20:04 UTC

* After the validations on stream creation, I have added function for accessing stream for admin actions which can be changing stream name, description, subscription, managing other stream admins etc. Which has concept:
             * Stream admin can always perform stream admin actions.
             * Real admin can always perform stream admin action on public stream. (Subscribed or unsubscribed)
             * Realm admin can perform stream admin actions on subscribed private stream. (Note that realm admin don't have to be stream admin, just subscribed to stream)

**Yashashvi Dave** · 2018-02-01 20:15 UTC

* After setting this function, add this in existing API points and add API points to get, add and remove stream admins. Which generally calls upper defined functions.

* After all this, again main validation is to prevent private stream without stream admin which also prevent private stream without subscribers. This concept may require some modifications. Strategy is,
     - Now, on both calls(to remove subscribers from stream or to remove stream admins) we check that after 
       removing the list of subscribers/stream admin from private stream, does private stream become without 
      admins? If yes, throw json error.

Now, to check this:
    - Differentiate subscribed realm admins to private stream and stream admin(who are not realm admin)
    - Find the no of stream admins and realm admins from the list of subscriber(passed as argument by user to 
      unsubscribe them from stream) and compare them with the existing no of subscribed realm admins and 
      stream admins. 
     - If all admins are removed then return json error, or if at least one stream admin or subscribed realm admin can  
       be part of stream after un-subscription return.

**Priyank Patel** · 2018-01-25 12:42 UTC

I have two PR up
[#8165](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/8165) is for webpack that does not output new bundle if files are not changed.

[#8157](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/8157) is for service worker to provided better caching for files we want, that will probably be likely to have lot of changes requested for python code since i worked on it for first time.

**Priyank Patel** · 2018-02-05 22:12 UTC

Once again if somebody could look at #8157 that would be great. As i posted on the PR. The page loading improvement is very significant.

Loading time of all the cached files by SW are 500ms +-100ms. Instant reload of the website after `onbeforeunload` handler. And saves a lots of traffic from reaching backend.

I labelled it WIP since i found some issue after testing it out today. Genrally i think i need to fix most of the python code.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-02-05 22:27 UTC

@cPhost why is the service worker approach preferable to using proper cache-control headers?

**Priyank Patel** · 2018-02-05 22:29 UTC

We can control when to renew cache. We are like a proxy in between user and the server this is just basic functionality it provides we can do a lot more.

Service Worker run apart from website's thread and we can also provide support for Push Notification and much more but the thing is not all browser's support it.

**Priyank Patel** · 2018-02-05 22:31 UTC

If we use proper cache-control headers we still provided solid caching, and we currently do :) but often what use might notice if that the page still loads slowly it's because the browser still revalides caches or dumps them all the time.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-02-05 22:33 UTC

I see, so it's basically forcing the browser to cache certain assets longer than it would normally.  Hmm.

**Priyank Patel** · 2018-02-05 22:34 UTC

Yep, once you add something it always would be there and never go away.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-02-05 22:34 UTC

I guess that could make sense to use for those asset files which have a hash in the name (and thus should never change)?

**Priyank Patel** · 2018-02-05 22:36 UTC

That does not matter since if one file is change the service worker would go out and fetch all the files again.

**Priyank Patel** · 2018-02-05 22:37 UTC

That happens in background and takes affect after user reloads.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-02-05 22:46 UTC

OK.  I'll need to think a bit more about this before I'm sure we want to do it, but that info is helpful!

#8223 is rather big, so I'm not asking for a timely full review. I am wondering, however, about an approach I took in the last commit two dynamically include HTML code with jinja. For context, this commit adds a list of embedded bot UI configuration fields to `settings_sidebar.html`.  The length of this list varies, so we need to include it dynamically, either with JS or a  template language (Jinja, since it's a html file rendered in the backend). Since an approach with a template language is preferable, I added the following code to `settings_sidebar.html`:
```.html
                    <div id="config_edit_inputbox">
                         {% block config_edit_inputbox_items %}
                             {% for bot in raw_page_params.realm_embedded_bots %}
                                 {% for key, value in bot.config.items() %}
                                 <div class="input-group" name="{{bot.name}}" id="{{bot.name}}_{{key}}_edit">
                                     <label for="{{bot.name}}_{{key}}_input_edit">{{key}}</label>
                                     <input type="text" name="{{key}}" id="{{bot.name}}_{{key}}_input_edit"
                                         maxlength=1000 value="" />
                                 </div>
                                 {% endfor %}
                             {% endfor %}
                         {% endblock %}
                     </div>
```

This code needs to access certain entries in page_params. Therefore, I added page_params to the jinja render call in `home.py`:
```.py
    response = render(request, 'zerver/index.html',
                      context={'user_profile': user_profile,
                               'page_params': JSONEncoderForHTML().encode(page_params),
                               'raw_page_params': page_params,     <--------------------------------------------------------------------------
                               'nofontface': is_buggy_ua(request.META.get("HTTP_USER_AGENT", "Unspecified")),
                               'avatar_url': avatar_url(user_profile),
                               'show_debug':
                               settings.DEBUG and ('show_debug' in request.GET),
                               'pipeline': settings.PIPELINE_ENABLED,
                               'show_invites': show_invites,
                               'is_admin': user_profile.is_realm_admin,
                               'show_webathena': user_profile.realm.webathena_enabled,
                               'enable_feedback': settings.ENABLE_FEEDBACK,
                               'embedded': narrow_stream is not None,
                               },)
```

My question is if this approach is acceptible regarding the change in home.py.

Generally the approach is that the backend mostly provides scaffolding kind of stuff, but the frontend dynamically builds the inner lists.

because the migration is in conflict with another migration. This happens when a new migration was merged to master and we forget to update our migration number and its dependency. ## PR #8365

*2018-03-08 to 2018-03-12 · 39 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/91-code-review/topic/PR.20.238365/with/530551)*

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-03-08 13:47 UTC

Requesting review for PR #8365 :)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-08 13:54 UTC

One quick thing, @Tarun Kumar: is it possible to do early-exit when this condition is `false`?

~~~
(user_groups.is_member_of(data.id, people.my_current_user_id()) || me.is_admin
~~~

We like early-exit because it keeps the code flatter, plus the diff is easier to read.

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-03-08 14:27 UTC

@Steve Howell can you specify the line number, as this line occurs many times?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-08 14:28 UTC

I think everywhere we could early-exit on that condition, we should.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-08 14:28 UTC

For the typeahead guard in particular, that's in a really long function that would be nice to split up or re-organize in early refactoring commits.

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-03-08 14:31 UTC

The problem was two different cases when the user groups page first loads and if the user removes himself/herself from a group then he/she is not allowed to modify that group, so I needed to add that condition in typehead also

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-08 14:31 UTC

Do you know what I mean by early-exit?

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-03-08 14:32 UTC

Not exactly, can you elaborate ?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-08 14:33 UTC

Instead of saying:

~~~ js
if (user_can_edit) {
    // lots and lots of code gets indented
}
~~~

do this:

~~~ js
if (!user_can_edit) {
    return;
}

// lots of code at original indent level

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-08 14:34 UTC

Even for the really long function, my theory is that if the user can't edit, we should not only be turning off typeahead, but we probably don't need to set up the pills, etc.

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-03-08 14:35 UTC

Oh got it, thanks @Steve Howell even I thought of so many deletions because of indentation.!
So. I will perform some refactoring in that case.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-08 14:35 UTC

sounds good!

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-08 14:38 UTC

Sometimes adding indentation is fine, of course, so there will still be judgment calls.  A good thing to do is extract smaller functions in early refactoring commits.  This will cause some indentation, but you can usually do those as pretty small commits.

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-03-08 14:40 UTC

I think that, the ajax calls should be kept in the way as such, I mean with the condition outside them, but for other stuff I think we can do the above modification!

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-08 14:42 UTC

Check this out:

https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/8624/commits/eafb013c72bcccdde8d4889b3ce791042e314303

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-08 14:43 UTC

JS is pretty nice about letting you have nested scopes like that.

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-03-08 14:43 UTC

Thanks for the details, I'll try do that!

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-08 14:48 UTC

@Tarun Kumar I have another suggestion...

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-08 14:49 UTC

Make a one-line function:

~~~ js
exports.can_edit = function (data, me) {
   return (user_groups.is_member_of(data.id, people.my_current_user_id()) || me.is_admin
}
~~~

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-03-08 14:50 UTC

and then call to check for it?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-08 14:50 UTC

yep, then you can say 

``` js
if (!exports.can_edit(data, me) {
  return;
}
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-08 14:50 UTC

And then you can also simplify the node tests.

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-03-08 14:51 UTC

good idea, thanks!

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-08 14:51 UTC

Toward the top test the function directly.

Then in the rest of the module you can just stub it:

~~~ js
settings_user_groups.can_edit = function () { return false; }
// test false cases

settings_user_groups.can_edit = function () { return true; }
// test true logic
~~~

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-03-08 14:52 UTC

sounds good!

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-08 14:53 UTC

:thumbs_up:

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-03-11 13:19 UTC

@Steve Howell the node tests are getting pretty complicated in the case of using early-on exit conditions, because there are two conditions both of which are to be tested, in a single go-through of settings_user_groups.js, which is making it difficult to test, do you have any hints how to accomplish that ?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-11 17:14 UTC

I think it can sometimes be helpful to structure your tests like this:

* top - have one function that tests your "ok to edit" function directly
* middle - mock "ok to edit" as true, and test all the "normal" scenarios
* end - mock "ok to edit" as false, and test the bail out scenarios (these are often smaller tests)

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-03-11 17:19 UTC

I tried to do that, but then either normal scenario was getting disturbed or the special case was, the problem is once settings_user_groups.set_up is called in the test file, testing either one of the scenario is exclusive in the sense that I can only test one of them, as flow of code changes in both situations bypassing the other code, am I correct thinking this, because I tried it, it doesn't seem to work.. :)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-11 17:21 UTC

you can probably call `set_up` multiple times in the test

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-11 17:22 UTC

or maybe call `populate_user_groups` multiple times

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-03-11 17:22 UTC

but then, the portion which anyway is going to be executed (intializing stuff) would be tested twice, second time to just set them as noop, to reduce redundancy.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-11 17:23 UTC

it's fine to do that

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-11 17:24 UTC

There are some places where we re-initialize zjquery several times.  There's really no harm in executing certain sections multiple times.

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-03-11 17:25 UTC

Ok, because I was able to think of that method only after trying out the other ones
Yeah, I wanted to make sure that if it was fine doing that.
Thanks @Steve Howell

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-11 17:25 UTC

Also, remember that JS functions don't actually get executed till you call them.  So running `populate_user_groups` doesn't really run the click handlers, it just "attaches" them.

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-03-11 17:26 UTC

I'll keep that in mind :)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-11 17:26 UTC

I would try to still be thoughtful about how you set things up (which led to your questions, I think), but don't feel overly constrained that you can run things only once.

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-03-12 10:34 UTC

PR #8365 is ready for review :)

## #9055

**Ben Reeves** · 2018-04-10 21:27 UTC

@Alyssa Wagenmaker and I plugged the coverage hole in `soft_deactivation.py` in #9055, but I'm feeling kinda lacking in understanding of this part of `soft_deactivation.py`:

```python
if (stream_subscription_logs[-1].event_type == 'subscription_deactivated' and
                stream_subscription_logs[-1].event_last_message_id < user_profile.last_active_message_id):
            # We are going to short circuit this iteration as its no use
            # iterating since user unsubscribed before soft-deactivation
            continue
```

Particularly this part of the conditional:

```python
stream_subscription_logs[-1].event_last_message_id < user_profile.last_active_message_id):
```

We traced through where those two fields are being updated, and we feel that it should perhaps read `<=` instead of `<`. We're also skeptical if this part of the conditional is actually necessary. When could `event_last_message_id` ever be greater than `last_active_message_id`, and how could that change things?

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-10 21:36 UTC

That case is for another user modifying your subscriptions.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-10 21:36 UTC

(E.g. another user creating a new stream and subscribing you to that new stream)

**Christian Höppner** · 2018-04-17 06:50 UTC

```

**Christian Höppner** · 2018-04-17 06:51 UTC

Although `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is a more organized approach, and cluttering the home folder with rc files is frowned upon by some people.

**Christian Höppner** · 2018-04-17 06:52 UTC

Since the file contains a piece of potentially sensitive information, some thought should be given to securing it as well.

**Michael Bologna** · 2018-04-17 16:55 UTC

So just to confirm, everyone agrees with using the `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` environment variable to store the single config file within '$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/zulip? Or are we using `$XDG_CONFIG_DIRS`? Also the config file is being renamed to `.zuliprc`, correct?

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-17 17:31 UTC

I think it's a little unclear whether we should be using `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`.  Like, that's definitely what we should be using if the config file were being managed by the terminal app.  But since it just stores data the user inputs, and most users don't know where XDG_CONFIG_HOME is (and sometimes that's not even set), I think we should be asking users to put their 3-line config file at `~/.zuliprc`, and have the app look there by default.  Otherwise the instructions for how to setup the app need to cover `XDG_CONFIG` environment variables, and I don't think that's either the intent of XDG or something I've seen anything else make you do.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-17 17:31 UTC

Reading https://specifications.freedesktop.org/basedir-spec/basedir-spec-0.6.html, it's pretty clearly intended for desktop apps where you configure your settings in a GUI, which isn't our terminal client.

**Armaan Ahluwalia** · 2018-05-17 19:17 UTC

@Tim Abbott Could you take a look at this PR. Fixed a bunch of conflicts and made necessary changes based on comments.

**Armaan Ahluwalia** · 2018-05-17 19:17 UTC

#9342

**Armaan Ahluwalia** · 2018-05-28 06:20 UTC

@Tim Abbott A reminder that #9342 is waiting on your review.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-28 06:23 UTC

@Armaan Ahluwalia I was actually just looking at that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-28 06:24 UTC

I'm still wondering whether we really need to do this whole `window.module_name = module_name` hack.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-28 06:24 UTC

It seems to me like we could instead just have have those modules declared as exposing their module name, right?

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-28 06:28 UTC

(The `window` system is fragile in that it can end up accidentally masking properties on the actual window object, so I do have good reason to not want to do that)

**Armaan Ahluwalia** · 2018-05-28 06:32 UTC

@Tim Abbott I actually did a bunch of work on this so I know from experience this is the right way to move forward. Reason being trying to expose variables using the loaders is a fragile system for the following reasons - 
1) Plugins such as expose-loader basically wrap modules in additional code that can cause conflicts with other plugins working correctly so in real fact it is a more fragile system than directly exposing the window global ( We shouldn't worry too much about this as its clear this is NOT the way to move forward only a transition step to webpack. The way to move forward is relying on module imports. )
2) Misdirection. It is more clear to the reader that window is being exposed as a global when looking at the file.
3) I actually did attempt what you suggest and I found it had a bunch of issues.

**Armaan Ahluwalia** · 2018-05-28 06:33 UTC

Also the compile time would be higher when wrapping each and every module using a loader

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-28 06:33 UTC

OK.  Another question: It looks like this duplicates code for the `common` bundle?

**Armaan Ahluwalia** · 2018-05-28 06:34 UTC

I'm sorry im currently rebasing

**Armaan Ahluwalia** · 2018-05-28 06:34 UTC

I missed your commits on sunday.

OK, no worries.

## asking for review

*2018-12-29 to 2018-12-29 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/91-code-review/topic/asking.20for.20review/with/676974)*

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-29 18:02 UTC

Just a quick note on using this stream.  If you simply need a review, there's no need to post here.  If you want to "bump" a review, it's worth taking a second to explain why it should be prioritized.  For example, you can say something like "this has been in the queue for three weeks, and the build passed".

It's also good to link both the issue and the PR and briefly state what the issue is about.  Stating what the issue is about can help reviewers besides Tim know that they should look at it, since different people have different expertise.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-29 18:04 UTC

I should also remind people that a great way to contribute is to review PRs. :smile: 

Even if you're not super confident in doing a "thorough" review, you can add value by hunting for typos, asking probing questions, and, most importantly, pulling down the PR and doing QA on it.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-29 18:04 UTC

I've been lax at this myself lately, so do as I say, not as I do. :wink:

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-29 18:05 UTC

https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pulls

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-29 22:05 UTC

I'll add that doing QA is a particularly good way for someone new to the project to contribute in this capacity, since anything you found confusing in trying to test the feature is useful information.  Even just testing a PR and posting "I played with it and it worked for me" is really helpful.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-05 19:41 UTC

I think the code is `$('#search_query')` here to get the stop words, which seems brittle to me.  I think it's easier to pull the search keywords from the query filter, not the widget.  Because of the way the code is structured, we are not really testing a lot.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-05 19:42 UTC

A second thing is that I generally just write a custom `append` method, which is why we've never added it to `zjquery`.  Basically, `append` is kind of complicated, and it's easier to stub it and just collect the values.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-05 19:45 UTC

It's also not clear why we're translating the search words.  I think that's almost certainly a mistake of copy/paste nature.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-05 19:46 UTC

Here is the patch that I used to fix the tests, without touching zjquery (i.e. drop the first commit):

~~~ js
$ git diff
diff --git a/frontend_tests/node_tests/narrow.js b/frontend_tests/node_tests/narrow.js
index 32e996f..97eca8a 100644
--- a/frontend_tests/node_tests/narrow.js
+++ b/frontend_tests/node_tests/narrow.js
@@ -156,9 +156,23 @@ run_test('show_empty_narrow_message', () => {
     narrow.show_empty_narrow_message();
     assert($('#non_existing_user').visible());

+    var display = $("#empty_search_stop_words_string");
+
+    items = [];
+    display.append = (html) => {
+        items.push(html);
+    }
+
+    // We may change the code to get this out of filters,
+    // but for now we need to simulate it.
+    $('#search_query').val('grail');
     set_filter([['search', 'grail']]);
     narrow.show_empty_narrow_message();
     assert($('#empty_search_narrow_message').visible());
+
+    assert.equal(items.length, 2);
+    assert.equal(items[0], ' ');
+    assert.equal(items[1].text(), 'translated: grail');
 });

~~~

    propagate_query = Q(recipient = message.recipient, subject = orig_topic_name)

    if propagate_mode == 'change_later':

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-26 19:25 UTC

@Tim Abbott Do you agree with me that we should have a max-id approach here for unstarring messages?  Or is that just overkill?  The race conditions are sort of unlikely and mostly harmless, so I could be swayed.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-26 19:27 UTC

My proposal is this:
* client gets maxed starred it
* server unstars with `<= max_id`
* server notifies clients `max_ids`
* client unstars with `<= max_id`

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-26 19:32 UTC

(I should point out my approach only saves races for starring **new** messages.  Completely avoiding the race would involve sending explicit list of ids, which might not be the end of the world.)

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-26 19:33 UTC

(And the "dumb" approach is to just have the server unstar everything, then the clients unstar everything, and any activity during the race window may be incorrectly reflected in the clients until the next reload.)

**Ruchit Vithani** · 2019-02-26 19:35 UTC

@Steve Howell  Won't it be the case in this example that instead of starring 13, user star message with ID 8, it will get unstarred then [Screenshot-2019-02-27-at-1.00.08-AM.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/e6/pNVzKrOv3x2OuzbqmsTb9i3U/Screenshot-2019-02-27-at-1.00.08-AM.png)

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-26 19:36 UTC

Yeah, you'd still have the race for old messages.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-26 19:37 UTC

Maybe the "dumb" approach here actually is best.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-26 19:39 UTC

@Ruchit Vithani I think in the current PR you're only implementing part of the solution I was trying to communicate.   Unless Tim responds here soon, it's probably fine to just use `exports.ids.clear()` and not deal with any max-id logic.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-26 19:40 UTC

FWIW I tested this out and it seems to work pretty well!

**Ruchit Vithani** · 2019-02-26 19:46 UTC

> @Ruchit Vithani I think in the current PR you're only implementing part of the solution I was trying to communicate. Unless Tim responds here soon, it's probably fine to just use `exports.ids.clear()` and not deal with any max-id logic.
 I also think, it will not cause any problem. Because, before sending event to server, we will call `exports.ids.clear()`, so that, if one stars some message after that time, it will not come under the action of `exports.ids.clear()`,(because it has already happened). 
We move in following manner
* User unstars all messages
*  We call `exports.ids.clear()`
* Backend flow occurs and server sends event
* Now, suppose before server responds, user stars some message. There does not seem any reason to me, that it will get unstarred (because, it will not be trapped by `exports.ids.clear()` at any point).

$(...).on('mouseover', ..., function(e) {

			{{else}}
			<span>{{name}}<br />{{status_text}}<br />Last online: {{last_seen}}</span>
			{{/if}}
		{{/if}}
	{{else}}
		{{#if is_away}}
		<span>{{name}}<br />Last online: Today</span>
		{{else}}
			{{#if online_now}}
			<span>{{name}}<br />{{last_seen}}</span>
			{{else}}
			<span>{{name}}<br />Last online: {{last_seen}}</span>
			{{/if}}
		{{/if}}
	{{/if}}
</div>
```
This template would have no reusability for other tooltips, unless we keep on adding if statements.
I know we want to avoid html in js as much as possible, but I think having this as is would be more economical for us.

## #12080

*2019-04-08 to 2019-04-10 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/91-code-review/topic/.2312080/with/729888)*

**Abhishek Kumar Singh** · 2019-04-08 03:11 UTC

@Tim Abbott  @Rohitt Vashishtha  Added a fix for the bullet-list-indicators, would be great if you could review it in your free time.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2019-04-08 06:12 UTC

Hey! Thanks for working on this @Abhishek Kumar Singh . It'd really help to see some test cases along with this change, ideally in `markdown-test-cases.json`.

Also, I'm not sure I understand how your code works. Can you explain how you debugged this?

**Abhishek Kumar Singh** · 2019-04-08 08:18 UTC

I used a lot of console.log statements to confirm all this,
First of all I checked this.rules.list and it's regex was altered to have `* ` in place of `[+*-]`,  so I explicitly used the `block.list` to exec() the same src, what I found out was it worked fine and we got bullet list as expected even after using - , + , then I traced back to the point where this regex was altered in `Lexer()` at the line `this.rules = block.tables;` and found out that by default we have tables as true and the tables change 3 things
* nptables
* tables
* list
and then I checked making tables, having the `block.list` explicitly I found out that it lead to failure in rendering the tables, so I got confirmed that the change in regex of list was intentional for the tables to work, 
What we needed to fix was
* Change the list to block.list whenever table is not encountered and it should check each line of the message not for the whole message at once
so I wrote it inside `while(src)`

**Abhishek Kumar Singh** · 2019-04-08 08:20 UTC

@Rohitt Vashishtha I mentioned everything I did while changing it hoping it's the correct way :sweat_smile: , thanks for reviewing it, I will add tests cases once I get back to hostel.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-04-10 00:28 UTC

@Abhishek Kumar Singh great, those notes are super helpful.  Generally you should try to communicate those details in your pull request (either as a comment or in the commit message), because they're essential to another developer understanding why you made the changes you made.

**Abhishek Kumar Singh** · 2019-04-10 01:00 UTC

thanks, I will keep it in my mind, will add it to my pr.

## #12154 - fix caching on render_markdown_path

*2019-04-18 to 2019-04-21 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/91-code-review/topic/.2312154.20-.20fix.20caching.20on.20render_markdown_path/with/734230)*

**Puneeth Chaganti** · 2019-04-18 03:30 UTC

Calls to `render_markdown_path` weren't getting cached since the `context`
argument is a `dict` and is unhashable.  This was causing some of the slowness Tim describes in #11055 in `test_urls.py` and `test_docs.py`.  

I've attempted to fix it by converting the dict args to tuples before caching, and back to dicts.  I'm not sure if this code is readable enough, or if there's a better way of doing this. Any comments and suggestions are welcome!

**Wyatt Hoodes** · 2019-04-18 06:15 UTC

Seems pretty clever to me, Puneeth! :)

**Puneeth Chaganti** · 2019-04-18 08:10 UTC

Not sure if *clever* is a good thing or a bad thing. :see_no_evil:

**Steve Howell** · 2019-04-18 16:07 UTC

@Puneeth Chaganti I think your implementation is fine, although I wonder if just a single custom decorator would be easier to understand than the three stacked decorators.

**Puneeth Chaganti** · 2019-04-18 16:10 UTC

I was thinking about that too. I wanted to leave the `ignore_unhashable_lru_cache` decorator, in case people wanted to use it elsewhere, but I'm not sure.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-04-18 16:23 UTC

> I was thinking about that too. I wanted to leave the `ignore_unhashable_lru_cache` decorator, in case people wanted to use it elsewhere, but I'm not sure.

I'm not sure how easily people would even find that decorator.  I also wonder if we should just fail hard if the arguments aren't hashable.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-04-18 16:28 UTC

For context, the original optimization was done in 59f61c25255f616064dc84d0ceb02f11e702ff4d.  It's possible that Umair didn't know enough about the underlying code to understand that the options were possibly always dicts that could be converted to hashable tuples.

I'm also kind of curious whether we ever get multiple results per instance of `markdown_file_path` during the lifetime of a server.  If not, then we could simply use `markdown_file_path` as the cache key.

**Puneeth Chaganti** · 2019-04-18 16:40 UTC

I'm not sure if we get multiple results per instance of `markdown_file_path` but that's an interesting idea. I'll investigate.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-04-18 16:58 UTC

@Puneeth Chaganti Cool, I think that investigation would be worthwhile.  It's possible that even if you determine that we always get the same data per value of `markdown_file_path`, we'll still want to make the cache key include all arguments, just so we can future-proof it in case there are future scenarios where we need to re-render paths based on data that changes during the lifetime of the server.

But it would still be interesting to know.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-04-21 18:59 UTC

Hmm, that's a really good thought.  @Puneeth Chaganti I think the answer is that we don't currently have a use case for passing different contexts for rendering the same article.  I could imagine that changing, however, if e.g. we had some template content that was reused (maybe included in a few different pages) and don't want to make that assumption.

## #12351 - css: Use SCSS nesting in reactions.scss.

*2019-05-18 to 2019-05-20 · 19 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/91-code-review/topic/.2312351.20-.20css.3A.20Use.20SCSS.20nesting.20in.20reactions.2Escss.2E/with/743341)*

**Vaibhav Rabber** · 2019-05-18 13:45 UTC

Here's a CSS rule that is completely useless in `reactions.scss`:

```css
.message_reactions .reaction_button:not(:only-child) {
    margin-bottom: 5px;
}
```

Since this is defined before the following:

```css
.message_reactions .message_reaction + .reaction_button {
    visibility: hidden;
    pointer-events: none;
    margin: 2px 0.1em 3px 0.1em;
    padding: 3px;
    height: 14px;
    border-radius: 4px;
    padding-left: 0.3em;
    border: 1px solid hsl(0, 0%, 73%);
    padding-right: 0.3em;
    float: left;
}
```

If `.reaction_button` is not the only child, the other children are `.message_reaction` only, which means the former rule is overridden. Should this be applied or removed?

**Vaibhav Rabber** · 2019-05-18 13:47 UTC

Also, if this needs to be applied, this can simply be merged in the later rule (since there is only one case when `.reaction_button` is visible)

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-18 21:46 UTC

@Vaibhav you should make sure you understand CSS precedence rules: Order of appearance in CSS files isn't the main precedence ordering.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-18 21:47 UTC

Looking at the commit that introduced that rule, c961172ab13d21bb427925a8777ddf911a54cbaf might be instructive as well.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-18 21:48 UTC

**Priyank Patel** · 2019-05-20 11:43 UTC

> Is CSS coverage testing a thing?

It sort of is but comes with it own challenges. You can use chrome devtools or puppeteer programmatically to get css coverage report.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-20 18:31 UTC

The challenge is that you need to exercise all the corner cases that might require the CSS in your tests in order for it to be really useful.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-20 18:31 UTC

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-05-20 22:11 UTC

That sounds like a good thing!

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-20 22:17 UTC

It depends what aspect of it you're thinking about.  I don't know of organizations that have high integration test (e.g. our Casper tests) coverage of their featureset, because that sort of test is slow, often flaky, and a lot of work to write.  Which is why our JavaScript codebase is primarily tested with our node unit test system (where we've been able to achieve really good coverage).

You should familiarize yourself with `git rebase`.  You can start an interactive rebase with `git rebase -i @~N` The `@~N` piece simply means "show me`N` commits up to and including `HEAD`(the most recent commit on your current branch)".             for user in good_users:
                context = common_context(user)
                context.update({
                    'email': user.delivery_email,
                })
                send_email('zerver/emails/find_team', to_user_ids=[user.id], context=context,
                           from_address=FromAddress.SUPPORT)
                if user.delivery_email not in emails_sent:
                    emails_sent.append(user.delivery_email)
            for email in set(emails).difference(emails_sent).difference(ignore_users):
                send_email('zerver/emails/find_team', to_emails=[email], context=None,
                           from_address=FromAddress.SUPPORT)
```

**Udit Krishna Chaudhary** · 2020-03-20 11:47 UTC

@Steve Howell

**Udit Krishna Chaudhary** · 2020-03-20 11:48 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-20 13:09 UTC

I would consider having a single function that parses the payload here.  Here is my untested code:

~~~ py
def get_topic_and_message(payload: str) -> Dict[str, str]:
    m = re.match('\[(.*?)\]\s+(.*)', payload)
    if not m:
        raise UnexpectedWebhookEventType('honeybadger', payload)
    return dict(
        topic=m.group(1),
        message=m.group(2),
    )
~~~

I've done all the changes and would maybe require a final review. But before that, I would like to discuss a problem I've faced here.
In `alert_words_in_realm` and `get_alert_word_automaton`, there's a decorator `@cache_with_key` that has a timeout parameter with value 3600*24. When I changed it to 0, the code changes in these functions were visible. But when I reverted it and pushed it, my tests failed (the same way it used to before). But if it was kept at 0, my tests passed. I tried it multiple times and this was the same result.

**Abhishek B Chakravarthi** · 2020-04-15 17:59 UTC

The test that failed was related to a very recent change I made in the function.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-15 18:02 UTC

@Abhishek B Chakravarthi It's possible that you're not clearing the cache correctly when things change, since you updated the model.

**Abhishek B Chakravarthi** · 2020-04-15 18:02 UTC

How do I do that? I'm not very familiar with this area.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-15 18:02 UTC

If you grep for `flush_user_profile`, you'll see how it clears the relevant alert word caches at the end of the function based on `alert_words` from `UserProfile`.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-15 18:03 UTC

If you look at that function and where it's called, you'll get a taste of what's involved.

**Abhishek B Chakravarthi** · 2020-04-15 18:04 UTC

I'll take a look and let you know. Thanks.

**Abhishek B Chakravarthi** · 2020-04-15 20:42 UTC

Yes, every commit should pass tests and additionally be a state we'd be happy to be the latest commit in master.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-19 00:06 UTC

A big part of the motivation is that it saves a ton of time for reviewers to merge the first N commits of a PR as soon as they're good, to avoid reading the same commit 5 times as one repeats review for the other parts of the PR.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-19 00:06 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-25 10:28 UTC

The way a failing test works is this:
* It should cover the exact scenario that is broken on master.
* It should fail on master.
* It should fail on master by asserting something that **should** be true on master but isn't.
* It should start to pass once you fix the "real" code.

* set up an outgoing webhook bot
* set up a stream
* do **not** subscribe the bot to the stream
* simulate sending an HTTP request to the outgoing bot with a message on that stream mentioning the bot
* assert that after that call, a new message has been written to the stream
